passage: After the last bell, Tarun gathered the boys under the neem tree behind the panchayat school. "From tomorrow, nobody talks to Anand. Not in cricket, not on the bus." "Why?" asked little Bholu. "He told Sir we were playing in the storeroom. He's a snitch. He deserves it." Tarun said it loudly, and the others nodded one by one. Tarun felt tall, like the tree. Everyone was looking at him, waiting for the next rule. Last year it was Tarun who'd eaten lunch alone for a month after he dropped a catch in the final. He remembered the empty bench. He pushed the memory down. This time he was on the inside. Next morning, when Anand came smiling to the pitch, Tarun turned his back first, and the rest turned after him.

qa.q: Where did Tarun gather the boys?
qa.a: Under the neem tree behind the panchayat school.

qa.q: Why did Tarun push the memory of the empty bench down?
qa.a: Remembering how lonely it felt would make it harder to shut Anand out, and he wanted to stay on the inside, safe from being left out again.

qa.q: At the neem tree, what choice could Tarun have made instead of a freeze-out?
qa.a: He could have talked to Anand about the storeroom complaint directly, rather than turning a grudge into a rule for the whole group.

qa.q: What might it be like for Anand to walk onto the pitch smiling and see everyone turn their backs?
qa.a: Anand would likely feel shocked and confused, as lonely as Tarun once felt on the empty bench.

grounding: A child organises a group to shun a classmate, feeling powerful and safe from being left out himself, and tells himself the target deserves it.

passage: In the lunchroom of the school on Maple Street, Amara slid a folded note along the table: "Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on." It moved from hand to hand. When Gabriel came with his tray, the chairs next to Amara's group were suddenly saved. He stood there, then sat at the end near the bins. Amara laughed a little too loudly at something Chloe said. It felt good, everyone following her note. Safer, too. Last week Chloe had whispered with Lily all through art, and Amara had spent the whole lesson wondering if she'd be next. Now nobody would leave her out; she was the one deciding. Anyway, Gabriel had copied her maths answers once, she told herself. He probably deserved it. She didn't look at the bins end again.

qa.q: What did Amara's note say?
qa.a: "Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on."

qa.q: What was Amara afraid of before she started the note?
qa.a: After Chloe whispered with Lily all through art, Amara worried about being the next one left out.

qa.q: What could Amara do the next time she feels that fear, instead of passing a note?
qa.a: She could tell a friend or a teacher she felt left out in art, dealing with her own worry instead of pushing it onto Gabriel.

qa.q: What is lunch like for Gabriel, sitting near the bins?
qa.a: He probably feels humiliated and confused, not knowing why the chairs were suddenly saved.

grounding: A child leads a lunchroom freeze-out, enjoying the power and safety it gives her, driven by her own fear of being left out.

passage: At the Saturday badminton club, Devika had a plan. "When Manjula asks to be partners, everyone's already paired. Okay?" The other three nodded, and Devika felt a warm rush, like winning a long rally. Manjula came in with her new racquet and asked Priti, then Roshni, then Gulnaz. "Sorry, already paired." She ended up hitting the shuttle against the wall alone. Devika told herself it was fair. Manjula showed off, didn't she, always talking about her state-level cousin. Besides, if the group wasn't against Manjula, it might be against someone else, and Devika had heard Priti call her own backhand "weak". Better to be the one choosing. Then Coach Dias, watching from the net, called Devika over. "Why is one player at the wall every week?" Devika's warm feeling drained away.

qa.q: Who did Manjula ask to be partners before hitting against the wall?
qa.a: Manjula asked Priti, then Roshni, then Gulnaz.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel a warm rush when the others nodded?
qa.a: Having the group follow her plan made her feel powerful and safe, the one choosing rather than the one chosen against.

qa.q: Coach Dias's question is a turning point. What honest choice could Devika make in answering it?
qa.a: Devika could admit she set it up and why, including her fear about the backhand comment, and ask how to put it right with Manjula.

qa.q: What might Saturdays feel like for Manjula, hitting against the wall alone?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels embarrassed and lonely, bringing a new racquet only to find every partner already taken.

grounding: A child who organises a club freeze-out feels powerful, excuses it as deserved, and is partly driven by fear of being the target herself.

passage: I'm Pranav, and I go to the same dance class as Lakshmi. She's eleven and the best at spins. Last month a new girl, Sana, joined and got the front spot in the show. The next week Lakshmi whispered to all the girls in the changing room, and after that nobody stood near Sana, nobody passed her the water bottle, nobody laughed at her jokes. Lakshmi walked in front of the group, chin up, and everyone copied her. I heard her say, "She thinks she's a star. She deserves it." But I also noticed she kept glancing back to check the others were still with her, and when one girl smiled at Sana, Lakshmi's face went tight. I don't know what she was scared of. Last year Lakshmi had been the new girl nobody talked to.

qa.q: What did Sana get in the show?
qa.a: She got the front spot in the show.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi's glances back at the group suggest?
qa.a: They suggest that under her confidence she was afraid of losing her place, needing to check everyone was still following her.

qa.q: What could a teacher or friend do to stop the freeze-out?
qa.a: Someone could talk to Lakshmi privately about how she felt last year as the new girl, and pair Sana with different dancers in practice.

qa.q: What is dance class like for Sana now?
qa.a: Sana is surrounded by girls who won't stand near her or laugh at her jokes, which likely makes her feel lonely and unwanted despite her front spot.

grounding: A girl leads a group in shunning a new dancer, feels powerful and says the girl deserves it, while seeming afraid of losing her own place.

passage:
Monday. Mohit, ten, stood in the school corridor with his gang. "From today, nobody talks to Baljeet. He told the teacher we were copying." The others nodded. Mohit felt strong, like the captain of a winning team.

Wednesday. Baljeet sat alone at lunch. Mohit watched his friend Aman look at Baljeet's lunch box, then at Mohit. Mohit felt a flicker of fear. What if Aman went to Baljeet's side? Then Mohit would be the one on his own. So he said loudly, "Anyone who sits with him is out too."

Friday. Aman sat with Baljeet anyway. Two more boys followed. Mohit stood with his tray and nobody beside him. For a moment, he knew exactly how Baljeet had felt all week.

qa.q: Why did Mohit say nobody should talk to Baljeet?
qa.a: He said Baljeet told the teacher they were copying.

qa.q: What was Mohit afraid of on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was afraid that if Aman went over to Baljeet, he himself would be the one left alone.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Mohit, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Standing alone with his tray showed him how Baljeet had felt; he could apologise to Baljeet and join Aman's table.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt choosing to sit with Baljeet?
qa.a: Aman was probably nervous about Mohit's threat but felt it was wrong to leave Baljeet alone, and Aman's choice gave others courage.

grounding: A boy organises a freeze-out of a classmate, feels powerful, and acts from fear of losing his own place, until he ends up alone.

passage: Gopika, you asked why I get upset when you talk about "not letting" a girl sit with your group. Let me tell you. I'm your Kunal mama. When I was eleven, there was a new boy, Manoj, who was good at everything, cricket, maths, jokes. My friends started liking him more than me. So I made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj. And they obeyed. Walking around with everyone doing what I said, I felt like a king. I told myself Manoj was a show-off who deserved it. But really, I was scared. If he took my place, where would I go? One day I saw him crying behind the bicycle shed. I felt sick. That evening I told my father, and he made me go to Manoj's house and apologise that same night. I've never forgotten either the power or the fear.

qa.q: What did Kunal tell his friends about Manoj?
qa.a: He made a rule: nobody talks to Manoj.

qa.q: What was Kunal really feeling behind the freeze-out?
qa.a: Kunal felt powerful, but underneath was scared of losing his place to Manoj.

qa.q: Why was going to Manoj's house to apologise a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It made Kunal face what he had done and take responsibility the same day, instead of hiding behind the story that Manoj deserved it.

qa.q: How might Manoj have experienced the freeze-out?
qa.a: Manoj likely felt hurt and lonely, which is why Kunal found him crying behind the bicycle shed.

grounding: An elder recalls leading a freeze-out of a classmate as a boy, feeling powerful while secretly fearing losing his own place.

passage: It was pouring on the school trip, and forty children were packed into one hall at the science museum, waiting for the rain to stop. Vasudha, ten, had spent the whole bus ride whispering to her group: "Don't sit with the new girl, Rhea. She thinks she's so smart." Now, in the hall, Rhea tried to join them on the mat. Vasudha shook her head, and the others turned their backs. Vasudha felt a little rush: they'd listened to her. Rhea sat alone near the door. Anand, from their class, looked at Vasudha. "Why are you doing this?" "She's a show-off," Vasudha said quickly. But the truth was, since Rhea came, Vasudha's best friend had started sitting with Rhea at lunch. Vasudha was afraid of being the one left out. The class teacher noticed Rhea alone and walked over.

qa.q: How many children were packed into the hall?
qa.a: Forty children were packed into one hall.

qa.q: What was Vasudha really afraid of?
qa.a: Vasudha was afraid of losing her best friend to Rhea and being the one left out herself.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do instead of freezing Rhea out?
qa.a: Vasudha could talk to her best friend about feeling left out, and include Rhea rather than turning others against her.

qa.q: What is it like for Rhea sitting alone near the door?
qa.a: Rhea likely feels hurt and lonely, shut out on a trip where everyone else has a group.

grounding: A child organises a group to shun a new classmate, feeling powerful while secretly afraid of losing her own place, during a rain-bound school trip.

passage: At the Lucknow colony's evening cricket, Preeti, eleven, stood by the stumps and announced, "Pankaj isn't playing. Nobody pass to him." The other kids nodded. Pankaj stood on the edge of the field, bat in hand. Preeti felt powerful. Everyone was listening to her. When her little cousin asked why, Preeti said, "He cheats." But she knew he didn't. The real reason was that yesterday, the older kids had picked Pankaj first instead of her, and she had felt, for a horrible moment, like she didn't belong. If he was out, she was safe. Pankaj walked home early, dragging his bat. Preeti watched him go and felt a strange twist in her stomach. Her grandmother, watching from the balcony, called her up and asked quietly, "What did that boy do?" Preeti had no answer.

qa.q: Why did Preeti say Pankaj couldn't play?
qa.a: Preeti said, "He cheats."

qa.q: What was Preeti really feeling behind the freeze-out?
qa.a: Preeti felt powerful on the surface but was afraid of not belonging after the older kids picked Pankaj first.

qa.q: What could Preeti's grandmother help her understand?
qa.a: Her grandmother could help Preeti see that excluding Pankaj came from fear, and encourage her to apologise and let him play.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt walking home early?
qa.a: Pankaj likely felt hurt and rejected, excluded without knowing the real reason.

grounding: A child who leads a group in shutting out a boy feels powerful but acts from fear of losing her own place, telling herself he deserves it.

passage:
"Hrithik, from today nobody talks to the new girl."
"Why, Gargi?"
"She acts like she knows everything. Everyone agreed."
"Everyone?"
"Everyone who's in our group. You're in, right?"
"...Yeah."
"Good. If she sits with us, we move."
"What did she actually do?"
"She answered every question in class. She wants to be teacher's pet."
"That's not so bad."
"Hrithik, do you want to be out too?"
"No."
"Then don't be difficult."
Gargi walked off feeling tall. If everyone was busy leaving the new girl out, nobody would leave her out. She pushed away a small thought: that the new girl's answers had been right.

qa.q: What did the new girl do in class, according to Gargi?
qa.a: She answered every question in class.

qa.q: Why did Gargi walk off feeling tall?
qa.a: She felt powerful and safe, believing that if everyone was busy shutting out the new girl, nobody would shut her out.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do instead of agreeing?
qa.a: He could refuse to join, talk to the new girl himself, or tell a teacher if the freeze-out goes on.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel when the group moves away from her?
qa.a: She would feel rejected and confused, not knowing what she did wrong.

grounding: Shows a child organising a group to shun a new classmate, feeling powerful and safe from exclusion, and telling herself the girl deserves it.

passage:
In Class 5, I led the freeze-out of Jahnavi. I'm Chandrika. I'm not proud of it.
Jahnavi had joined our group of four. My best friend started sitting with her at lunch. I felt a cold fear: what if they left me out?
So I told the others Jahnavi had laughed at us behind our backs. It wasn't true. For two weeks, we didn't speak to her. When she sat down, we got up.
I felt strong. The others listened to me. And I kept telling myself she deserved it.
One day I saw her eating alone behind the water tank. She was crying and pretending she wasn't. I felt sick, but I still didn't stop.

qa.q: Where did Chandrika see Jahnavi eating alone?
qa.a: Chandrika saw her eating alone behind the water tank.

qa.q: What made Chandrika start the freeze-out?
qa.a: Chandrika felt a cold fear of being left out when the best friend started sitting with Jahnavi.

qa.q: What could Chandrika have done when feeling that fear?
qa.a: Chandrika could have talked to the best friend about feeling left out, or told a teacher, instead of turning the group against Jahnavi.

qa.q: What was it like for Jahnavi during those two weeks?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt lonely and hurt, eating alone and crying while pretending not to.

grounding: Shows a child leading a freeze-out out of fear of losing their place, feeling powerful and telling themselves the target deserved it.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 6A
For a week, Sarika has been eating alone. Today I found out why. Nirmala, who is very popular, has told the other girls not to talk to Sarika. When Sarika joins a game, the girls walk away.
I spoke to Nirmala alone. She wasn't sorry at first. "Sarika copies everything I do. She deserves it." Then she added, quietly, "If I don't lead, they'll drop me instead."
She looked scared when she said that.
I've spoken to Sarika's parents today and will pair the girls for a class project next week. I'll also meet Nirmala again. She needs to feel safe without pushing anyone out.

qa.q: How long has Sarika been eating alone?
qa.a: For a week.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's quiet comment suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels scared of being dropped herself, and leading the freeze-out makes her feel safe and powerful.

qa.q: How might the teacher's plan help both girls?
qa.a: Talking to Sarika's parents, pairing the girls in a project and meeting Nirmala again can rebuild trust and help Nirmala feel secure without excluding anyone.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika when the girls walk away?
qa.a: Sarika feels rejected and alone, left out of every game she joins.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a child who leads a freeze-out, saying the target deserves it, while acting from fear of losing her own place.

passage:
25 Dec, winter camp
Today I told everyone at the dorm not to talk to Yogesh. He showed the counsellor the pillow mess and we all got a warning. So I said, "Nobody sit with him at breakfast." And nobody did. It felt good. Like I was the one in charge, finally, and everyone listened. He deserved it. He's a snitch. But then at the bonfire, Rishi said, "Jeevan, if you tell on us, we'll do the same to you," and laughed, and I laughed too but my stomach dropped. Maybe that's why I did it. So it's him and not me. Yogesh ate alone again at dinner. He kept looking at the door. I don't feel that good now.

qa.q: What did Yogesh show the counsellor?
qa.a: The pillow mess.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan's stomach drop at the bonfire?
qa.a: Jeevan felt afraid, realising the group could turn on Jeevan just as easily, and suspects that fear is why the freeze-out happened.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to put things right?
qa.a: Jeevan could sit with Yogesh at breakfast, tell the others to stop, and talk to the counsellor about the freeze-out.

qa.q: If you were Yogesh, what would the day feel like?
qa.a: It would feel lonely and frightening, eating alone and watching the door, for having told the truth about the mess.

grounding: Shows a child who leads a group to shun a classmate feeling powerful, claiming the target deserves it, and acting from fear of being excluded.

passage: The Diwali holidays had brought every cousin back to the village, and the cricket ground by the pond was crowded. Imran was captain, as always. When Chetan walked up with his bat, Imran said loudly, "No teams for him. He cheated last time." He hadn't, really; he'd just argued a run-out. But the other boys laughed and turned their backs, and Imran felt tall, like the ground belonged to him. Then his older cousin arrived from the city, a better batsman, and the boys crowded around him instead. Imran's chest tightened. He glanced at Chetan sitting alone under the neem tree. Keeping Chetan out had felt like keeping himself in. Now he wasn't so sure it had worked.

qa.q: Where was the cricket ground?
qa.a: By the pond.

qa.q: Why did Imran's chest tighten when his cousin arrived?
qa.a: He felt anxious about losing his place as the boys crowded around the better batsman, the same fear that pushed him to shut Chetan out.

qa.q: What could Imran do now?
qa.a: He could invite Chetan to bat and admit to the boys that it was only an argument over a run-out, not cheating.

qa.q: What is it like for Chetan under the neem tree?
qa.a: He probably feels lonely and humiliated, excluded for an argument everyone treats as cheating.

grounding: Illustrates a child leading a group to shun a classmate, feeling powerful and acting from fear of losing his own place.

passage: In Tromsø, the polar nights made recess short and cold, and the class played snow football in the dark under floodlights. Lars always picked teams. This week he whispered to everyone, "Nobody picks Bilal." Bilal had scored against Lars's team twice. Now, each recess, Bilal stood by the fence, kicking snow, while Lars shouted names. Lars liked how quickly they obeyed. It felt safe, being the one who decides. He told himself Bilal was a show-off anyway. But on Thursday, when a new boy scored a beautiful goal and everyone cheered him instead of Lars, Lars felt a cold jolt. The teacher had noticed Bilal at the fence and called Lars aside after recess. "Tell me how teams get picked," she said.

qa.q: How many times had Bilal scored against Lars's team?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What did Lars feel when everyone cheered the new boy?
qa.a: He felt a cold jolt of fear, worried about losing his own place at the centre, which hints at why he shut Bilal out.

qa.q: How could the teacher help after asking about team-picking?
qa.a: She could make team choices fair, such as rotating captains, and talk with Lars about how Bilal feels at the fence.

qa.q: How does Bilal experience recess this week?
qa.a: He stands alone by the fence kicking snow, likely feeling rejected and confused about why nobody picks him.

grounding: Shows a child organising a group to exclude a classmate, enjoying the power and acting from fear of losing his own position.

passage: At the summer cricket camp, Chetan had a rule for the boys in his batch: nobody sits with Pradeep. "He's a show-off. He bowled me out on purpose," Chetan said, though everyone knew bowling people out was the whole point. Soon the lunch bench had a gap at one end, where Pradeep ate alone. Chetan liked how the others looked at him before deciding where to sit. It felt like being captain. But at night he thought about last year at his old school, when he was the one eating alone. If Pradeep got popular, Chetan might end up there again. So on Thursday, when Pradeep waved at him, Chetan turned away quickly, before anyone could see him wave back.

qa.q: Why did Chetan say Pradeep was a show-off?
qa.a: Because Pradeep bowled him out on purpose.

qa.q: What is Chetan afraid of at night?
qa.a: He is afraid that if Pradeep becomes popular, he will end up eating alone again, as he did at his old school.

qa.q: How could a coach at the camp break up the freeze-out?
qa.a: The coach could mix lunch groups and practice pairs, speak privately with Chetan about the rule, and check in kindly with Pradeep.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep on the lunch bench?
qa.a: It is lonely and confusing to eat alone at the end of the bench, shut out for playing well.

grounding: A boy who organises his batch to shun a classmate feels powerful and safe, acting from fear of being left out again himself.
